newsitem.title: JAPAN: China defence outlay rise no threat - Japan analysts.
newsitem.headline: China defence outlay rise no threat - Japan analysts.

text.p: Despite a planned sharp increase this year, China's defence outlays pose no major threat to its neighbours except for Taiwan, Japanese military analysts said on Monday.
"Besides the obvious exception of Taiwan, the growth in China's defence spending is no threat to other countries," said military affairs author Haruo Fujii.

China said on Sunday that defence spending in its 1997 budget would increase by 14.7 percent to 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion) from the 1996 budgeted figure, compared to growth of 11.3 percent in 1996.
The figure was also well above China's inflation goal of 6.0 percent for this year.

China's latest figure for defence spending is roughly one-fifth of Japan's military budget, and comparisons must also take into account the size of the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army, analysts said.

"The figure is modest when inflation and the size of the armed forces are taken into account. China is trying hard to achieve parity, not to overtake, the rest of the modern world in military technology," Fujii told Reuters.

But Naoaki Murata, vice minister at Japan's Defence Agency, told reporters Japan "must keep a watchful eye" on China's defence buildup, which he said included expansion of nuclear potential, modernisation of air and naval forces and an increase in the scope of its naval activities.

Another military analyst, Kazuhisa Ogawa, warned against exaggerating China's military might. "As usual there will be some Japanese media over-reacting to China's defence spending, but I don't think this should be treated like 'Peter and the Wolf'," Ogawa said in a telephone interview.

Fujii said China's latest military budget, coming on the heels of the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, is a political statement intended for both domestic and foreign audiences that the Chinese leadership is truthfully carrying out Deng's policy of modernising its armed forces.
The onus was on Japan and the United States to keep their promises of "engagement" with China rather than "containment", both analysts said.
"As long as Japan and the United States maintain high-level political dialogue, China's military will not become a threat," Ogawa said.
"If and when China becomes an economic superpower, Japan and the United States must make sure China does not become, or rather does not feel the need to become, a military superpower," Ogawa said.
India and Southeast Asia should not make too much of the growth in China's defence budget, they said.
"ASEAN has successfully localised the quarrel with China over the Spratly Islands and I'm sure they will maintain their cool, practical approach," Fujii said.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) groups Vietnam, Brunei, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
China, Taiwan, Brunei, the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia claim part or all of the islets in the South China Sea.

Ogawa said Sino-Indian security relations have been settled ever since 1988, when India warned China that it was compelled to adopt a nuclear deterrent against Beijing's nuclear arms. "That drove home the point that India wanted a stable security relation with China and this has worked very well," he said.

As for Taiwan, Fujii said the Chinese military was still not strong enough to mount an invasion. "The only thing China is capable of doing is a blockade, but even that is a remote possibility," he said.
